doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: Selling a Safeway jingle melody for $500
summary: He improvised a melody at a jingle house for a non-union buyout that became a ten-year national spot, and says he would not do that now.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: with like 75% of it, so I got all these checks for $172 and change, 50 of them. And then the next day, another 50 showed up. And I’m going we can just keep this going, I don’t mind signing these things. I was getting pissed off, I had to go buy a stamp. Like can’t they just put this in one check? It’s a first world problem you know. So but those kind of things are few and far in between for a commercial jingle. And I’ll tell you one more funny story about a commercial that I did, for Safeway as well. And they used to have these jingle houses here, and they still exist, but we would go do demos for them. So you’d go to this place and there’s be ten composers there and they’re all trying to get this jingle, whatever it is, a Coke commercial or whatever. So they might need trumpet and you’d go from room to room and you would play for these different things. And if one of them got it you’d get called back to do the final, and you’d get paid for the demo, whatever that would be you know. And I’m trying to remember the little lick I played for the Safeway thing though — God I’m forgetting it now. But anyway this little riff went like [scats] I’m singing actually a radio ID now, but it was something like that. And there was no music. And he goes can you just play a little melody kind of thing, can you come up with something? Oh yeah. How about this? And so I played this thing and he goes, “Oh that’s perfect.” And it was a thing that didn’t resolve, it went like [scats] and it never went [scats]. And he goes that’s perfect. Well that particular commercial was a buyout. And they gave me $500 to do this. “Hey would you do this non-union” which I usually don’t do. This was many many years ago though. $500. So I made $500 bucks. Man, all right. It took me 20 minutes. I’ll take that you know. Well that commercial became their national spot and ran for ten years. And not only did they use my melody, so I’m actually the composer, which I never got paid for, which would have equaled lots of dollars. They had different instrumentalists coming in and playing it over the years, probably just to buy-out with them too. Like a saxophone player playing my lick, an opera singer singing my lick. And so every time I’d hear it I just went [gags] you know. What did we learn? I could have probably retired off the money I would have made on this if I was the composer, if I was credited as the composer. It’s funny that I can’t think of how it went anymore.
I think it’s a mental block. You don’t want to torture yourself anymore.

So if somebody wants to just pay you for a buy out I mean I wouldn’t do that now anyway, just ‘cause I don’t need to do that anymore. But at the time man, $500 is a lot of money and yeah, I’ll do that. And now when it comes to a commercial jingle if you’re going to buy me out it’s going to cost you a lot more than that, especially if I’m going to make up the part you know, and I’m going to risk getting in trouble with the union. So I don’t really do that. It’s got to be on a union contract and be right.
